title: Modern built-in generics syntax
prompt_markdown: In modern Python (3.9+), what is the idiomatic way to type hint a function parameter as a dictionary mapping strings to lists of integers?

content.explanation: PEP 585 enabled standard built-in collections `dict` and `list` to act as generic type hints directly using square brackets: `dict[str, list[int]]`.

title: Runtime enforcement of type hints
prompt_markdown: What happens at runtime if you execute `val: int = 'hello world'` in standard CPython without third-party libraries?
hints: Does Python's runtime interpreter check annotations?

choices: Raises a TypeError immediately upon variable assignment
CPython successfully assigns the string to val without any error
The string is automatically coerced to an integer
content.explanation: Type annotations in Python are pure metadata stored in `__annotations__`. CPython does not enforce them at runtime; assigning a string to `val: int` succeeds without error.

title: Difference between Any and object
prompt_markdown: What is the key difference between `typing.Any` and `object` in static type checking?
hints: Which one bypasses the type checker entirely?

choices: They are exact synonyms in mypy and pyright
`Any` turns off type checking allowing any operation, while `object` requires narrowing before accessing attributes
`object` only accepts classes, while `Any` accepts primitives
`Any` causes runtime type checks, while `object` does not
content.explanation: `Any` acts as a dynamic escape hatch that allows any attribute access or call without checking. `object` is the safe root of the hierarchy; static checkers forbid calling arbitrary methods on it without narrowing via `isinstance()`.

title: Diagnose unhandled Optional attribute error
prompt_markdown:
A static checker flags an error on line 4: `Item "None" of "User | None" has no attribute "email"`. Diagnose why the checker flags this and write the corrected code.

```python
def notify_user(user_id: int, user_repo: dict[int, User]) -> None:
    user: User | None = user_repo.get(user_id)
    send_email(user.email, 'Welcome!')
```
hints: What happens if user_id is missing from user_repo?

rubric: Explains that `user` can be `None` when `user_id` is missing
Identifies that calling `.email` on `None` raises an `AttributeError` at runtime
Provides the corrected implementation with an explicit `if user is None:` guard
content.reference_answer:
Defect: `user_repo.get()` returns `None` if the ID is missing. Directly accessing `user.email` risks `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'email'`. The static checker enforces checking for None.
Corrected implementation:
```python
def notify_user(user_id: int, user_repo: dict[int, User]) -> None:
    user: User | None = user_repo.get(user_id)
    if user is None:
        raise ValueError(f'User {user_id} not found')
    send_email(user.email, 'Welcome!')
```

title: Explain boundary validation vs static typing
prompt_markdown: Explain to an interviewer why static typing alone cannot replace runtime validation (like Pydantic or Marshmallow) at web API boundaries.
hints: Where do external HTTP requests come from and when do static linters run?

rubric: Explains that static type checkers only inspect source code before deployment
Explains that external network payloads (JSON strings, query params) enter dynamically at runtime
Concludes that runtime parsing and validation libraries are mandatory to sanitize external untrusted input
content.reference_answer: Static type checking (via mypy/pyright) operates purely at build/lint time on Python source code, verifying developer logic assumptions. In contrast, external HTTP requests arrive over the network as raw JSON or strings at runtime from untrusted clients. Because Python does not execute static checks on incoming network payloads, runtime parsing and validation libraries (like Pydantic) are mandatory to inspect types, validate constraints, and reject malformed data before internal business logic runs.
